summary.text: A seiche is a standing wave in a fully or partly enclosed body of water, seen in places from swimming pools and harbours to lakes and seas.
Wind, air pressure changes, earthquakes or tsunamis disturb the water, and as gravity pulls it back toward level the motion reflects off the basin's ends and forms a standing wave.
Its rhythm is set by the basin's size, depth, contours and water temperature, so Lake Geneva swings on a 73-minute cycle while the North Sea takes about 36 hours.

facts.label: Lake Erie extremes
facts.value: Up to 5 metres between the lake's ends

items.prompt: A distant earthquake shakes your town, and water sloshes over the edges of your backyard swimming pool. What is happening?

options.label: A tsunami has travelled inland into the pool
Falling air pressure is sucking the water upward
The shaking has warmed the water so it expands
The tremors match the pool's resonance, setting up a seiche

items.explain: Pools are prone to quake seiches because ground tremors often match the resonant frequencies of small bodies of water.

items.prompt: Why can a seiche form in a lake but not on a wide-open stretch of ocean with no boundaries?

options.label: Open ocean water is too salty to slosh
The wave must reflect off the basin's edges to stand
Wind never blows steadily over open ocean
Gravity is weaker over very deep water

items.explain: The water must be at least partly bounded so that reflections off the basin's ends can build a standing wave.

items.prompt: In a sloshing seiche, some points on the surface do not rise or fall at all. What are they?

options.label: Nodes left by the repeated reflections
Crests where the water piles up highest
The two shores at each end of the basin
Spots where the water is deepest

items.explain: Repeated reflections produce standing waves with one or more nodes, points with no vertical motion.

items.prompt: Lake Erie is especially prone to wind-driven seiches. What makes it so?

options.label: It is the deepest and coldest of the Great Lakes
It sits right on top of an active fault
It is shallow and its long axis lines up with prevailing winds
It has no rivers flowing in or out of it

items.explain: Its shallowness and northeast–southwest stretch, which often matches the prevailing winds, maximise the winds' fetch.

items.prompt: A harbour's natural seiche period is 60 minutes. What is the period of its second harmonic?

options.label: 120 minutes
30 minutes
20 minutes
60 minutes

items.explain: The second harmonic's period is half the natural period, the third a third of it, and so on.

items.prompt: The word 'seiche' traces back to a Latin word for 'dry'. What is the link?

options.label: When the water pulls back, the shore is left exposed
Seiches mostly happen during summer droughts
The waves are too small to splash anyone
Early lakes that had them later turned to desert

items.explain: As the water recedes, the beach dries, which is where the name is thought to come from.

paragraphs.heading: Water rocking in a basin
paragraphs.text: A seiche is a standing wave set up in a body of water that is closed in or partly closed in. Seiches have been seen on lakes, reservoirs, swimming pools, bays, harbours, caves and seas. The one thing a seiche needs is boundaries on at least some sides, so that the standing wave can form. The shape does not have to be regular: even oddly shaped harbours swing back and forth at very steady frequencies.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The Swiss hydrologist François-Alphonse Forel popularised the word in 1890, after making the first scientific observations of seiches in Lake Geneva. People in the region had apparently used it for a long time for the rocking of alpine lakes. It is a Swiss French dialect word said to come from the Latin siccus, meaning dry, because the beach dries out as the water draws back.

paragraphs.heading: How a seiche works
paragraphs.text: A seiche starts when something disturbs the water, most often wind or shifts in air pressure, but also earthquakes or tsunamis. Gravity then pulls the surface back toward level, and the up-and-down motion sends a pulse along the basin at a speed set by the water's depth. The pulse bounces off the far end, and repeated reflections build a standing wave with one or more nodes, spots where the surface does not move up or down. How often the water rocks depends on the basin's size, depth and contours and on the water temperature. Besides the slowest, natural rhythm, higher harmonics appear: the second takes half as long per cycle, the third a third as long, and so on.

paragraphs.heading: Slow, steady rhythms
paragraphs.text: Seiches are often invisible to the eye, because each swing takes so long that even people in boats may not notice one. Low, rhythmic seiches are nearly always present on larger lakes, hidden among ordinary waves except in unusually calm spells. Forel found that Lake Geneva rocks lengthwise on a 73-minute cycle and crosswise in about 10 minutes. Lake Wakatipu in New Zealand raises and lowers its surface at Queenstown by 20 centimetres every 27 minutes, and the North Sea often rocks lengthwise about once every 36 hours.

paragraphs.heading: Seiches on the Great Lakes
paragraphs.text: Lake Erie is especially prone to wind-driven seiches because it is shallow and stretches northeast to southwest, often lining up with the prevailing winds. There, seiches of up to 5 metres can build between the two ends of the lake. The effect resembles a hurricane storm surge, except that a seiche can keep rocking across the lake for some time. On 13 July 1995 a seiche on Lake Superior dropped and then raised the water by one metre within fifteen minutes, leaving some boats dangling from docks by their mooring lines. On 26 June 1954 a 3-metre seiche hit Chicago's waterfront on Lake Michigan and swept eight fishermen off piers to their deaths.

paragraphs.heading: Shaken from far away
paragraphs.text: Seiches set off by earthquakes can appear thousands of miles from where the quake struck. Swimming pools are especially prone, since the shaking of the ground often matches the resonant frequencies of small basins of water. The 1994 Northridge earthquake made pools spill over across southern California, and Alaska's 1964 Good Friday earthquake set off seiches in pools as far away as Puerto Rico. The 1755 Lisbon earthquake stirred seiches 2,100 kilometres farther north, in Scottish lochs including Loch Ness and in canals in Sweden.
